parole.significato: to smell a rat; to have suspicions that everything is not quite alright and that there may be more to it than meets the…
parole.testo: Partly a corruption of the Danish expression ugler i mosen (“owls in the marshes”) which hints of dangers ahead. Literally, “To sense owls in the marsh.”

parole.significato: common hornbeam, Carpinus betulus
parole.testo: Borrowed from Danish avnbøg, from Middle Low German hagenboke. Cognate of German Hagebuche.

parole.significato: authorize
parole.testo: Borrowed from Danish bemyndige. By surface analysis, be- + myndig + -a.

parole.significato: a car (automobile)
parole.testo: From Danish bil.

parole.significato: mercury (spurge of the genus Mercurialis)
parole.testo: From Danish bingel, from German Bingel(kraut).

parole.significato: An incessant wind; a dated form of blåst
parole.testo: Calque of Danish blæst, Norwegian blest or Elfdalian bläst.

parole.significato: Bokmål (language)
parole.testo: From bok + mål, from the Danish bogmaal used in Norway since the 1850s to mean written standard language as opposed to dialects. Since 1929 this has been the official name for the written language, which was previously known as riksmål.

parole.significato: to shape, to create, to educate
parole.testo: Borrowed from Danish danne, from Middle Low German dan (past participle of don), from Proto-Germanic *dōną. Cognate of German tun and English do.

parole.significato: uniform, homogeneous
parole.testo: Borrowed from Danish ensartet. By surface analysis, en + -s- + -artad.

parole.significato: Old Norse (language of Scandinavia before ~1400 C.E.)
parole.testo: Calque of Danish oldnordisk, equivalent to forn + nordisk + -a.

parole.significato: that (correctly) predicts future developments (and plans for them)
parole.testo: fram + -synt. Probably borrowed from Danish fremsynt or Norwegian Nynorsk framsynt during 18th and 19th centuries.

parole.significato: a postage stamp
parole.testo: Calque of Danish frimærke. Compound of fri (“free”) + märke (“mark”). Meaning that it marked the letter as free to receive; as formerly it was the receiver who paid for postage. First attested in 1853.

parole.significato: boisterous partying, carousing, revelry, whooping it up
parole.testo: Borrowed from Danish galej.

parole.significato: gemütlich
parole.testo: From Danish gemytlig or German gemütlich, equivalent to gemyt + -lig.

parole.significato: dead serious
parole.testo: From Danish gravallvorlig, equivalent to grav + allvar + -lig. Attested since 1919. Compare German todernst.

parole.significato: a pastry consisting of a filling made out of eggwhites coated with chocolate and often covered in coconut flakes: a cho…
parole.testo: Compound of grädde (“cream”) + bulle (“bun”). Possibly a calque of Danish flødebolle.

parole.significato: synonym of hage (“pasture”)
parole.testo: Likely unadapted borrowing from Danish have.

parole.significato: In any order; impromptu; randomly; willy-nilly; without planning or thought.
parole.testo: Compound of hipp + som (“as”) + happ. Unadapted borrowing from Danish hip som hap, borrowed from Low German hippen (“hop”). According to SO attested since 1916. Compare with the rhyming structure of pick och pack (“bag and baggage”) and hugget som stucket (“same difference”).

parole.significato: sob
parole.testo: Onomatopoeic. Sense influenced by Danish hulke.

parole.significato: hygge
parole.testo: Borrowed from Danish hygge

parole.significato: assign, class, classify
parole.testo: Borrowed from Danish henføre or German hinführen. By surface analysis, hän (“away”) + föra (“steer”). Regarding shift in senses, compare English carry away.

parole.significato: An autumn and winter apple cultivar, with firm sweet and tart yellowish-white flesh, whose waxy skin is mostly deep red…
parole.testo: Unadapted borrowing from Danish Ingrid Marie. Compound of Ingrid + Marie. Coined by Danish teacher Carl Madsen c. 1910 after his deceased daughter.

parole.significato: Law of Jante
parole.testo: Partial calque of Danish janteloven. By surface analysis, Danish Jante (a fictional small Danish town) + lag (“law”).

parole.significato: basic idea; principal notion of how something should be
parole.testo: By surface analysis, kung + -s- + tanke. Possibly borrowed from Danish kongstanke, originally from the 1863 play The Pretenders by Norwegian playwright Henrik Ibsen. First attested in 1905.

parole.significato: to force into submission; to subdue, to suppress
parole.testo: Unknown. Possibly from Danish kue or Old Norse kúga. Possibly formed from Swedish kuv (“curve”), as in the English verb stoop. Compare origin of English cow (“intimidate”).

parole.significato: a kitchen midden; a prehistoric pile of waste
parole.testo: Borrowed from Danish køkkenmødding, compound of køkken (“kitchen”) + mødding (“midden”). Coined by Danish zoologist and geologist Japetus Steenstrup. According to SAOB and SO attested since 1873.

parole.significato: livelihood, day job, the source of income one lives from
parole.testo: From Danish levebrød, from leve (“live”) + brød (“bread”), equivalent to leva + bröd.

parole.significato: a schnapps; a small ammount of strong liquor, typically aquavit or another clear liquor, served in a shot glass
parole.testo: Unadapted borrowing from Danish lille en. Compound of Danish lille (“little”) + en (“one”).

parole.significato: cuff on the ear, bitch-slap
parole.testo: From Danish lussing.

parole.significato: with a keen ear
parole.testo: Likely borrowed from Danish lydhør, a compound of lyd (“sound”) + hør (“hear”). Compare German hellhörig.

parole.significato: value added tax
parole.testo: From Danish moms, an abbreviation of merværdiomsætningsafgift.

parole.significato: to have it nice and cozy; to enjoy oneself, to feel cozy, etc.
parole.testo: Attested since 1640. From Danish myse (“squint”) and Norwegian myse (“squint”), ultimately related to Ancient Greek μύω (múō, “to close ones lips/eyes”) and μυωπία (myopía, “near-sightedness; myopia”) and English myopic. Compare myssla (“to whistle; to squeak”, archaic, dialectal).

parole.significato: oatmeal ball; a kind of confectionery with oatmeal, cocoa, and butter, rolled into inch-size balls
parole.testo: neger (“negro (with similar sense development to English)”) + boll (“ball”). Possibly a calque of Danish negerbolle.

parole.significato: to move closer (to), to approach
parole.testo: From närmare (“nearer”), comparative of nära (“near”), likely influenced by Danish nærme.

parole.significato: environment, surroundings (relative to someone, often including the inhabitants as well)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Danish omverden, from German Umwelt. Attested since 1892.

parole.significato: a pawl (a pin in a ratchet gear)
parole.testo: From Danish pal or Low German pall, ultimately from Dutch pal.

parole.significato: a type of Vienna sausage with red casing, often seen as traditional Danish
parole.testo: Unadapted borrowing from Danish pølse (“sausage”). Doublet of pölsa. Red Vienna sausage sense attested since 1929, dialectal sense is older.

parole.significato: diamond (card of the diamonds suit)
parole.testo: From Danish ruder, from Middle Low German rûte. Cognate of German Raute (“rhombus”). Doublet of ruta.

parole.significato: nautical mile, now exactly 1,852 meters but (historical) previously roughly four times as much, 4 minutes of arc or ¹⁄₁…
parole.testo: From Danish sømil, from sø (“sea”) + mil (“Danish mile or league”). Equivalent to sjö + mil.

parole.significato: a Danish-style sandwich with a lot of topping (more than is usual on Swedish sandwiches), smørrebrød
parole.testo: From Danish smørrebrød (“sandwich”).

parole.significato: wrong-way driver, ghost driver
parole.testo: Calque of Danish spøgelsesbilist. Compound of spök- (“ghost”) + bilist (“autoist”).

parole.significato: A large street or path, particularly for pedestrians.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Danish strøg. Doublet of stryk.

parole.significato: noise, hullabaloo
parole.testo: Borrowed from Danish ståhej. Attested since 1886.

parole.significato: a sudden sound caused by an object knocking or lightly hitting something
parole.testo: stöt + ljud (“sound”). In the phonological sense, stöt is here a semantic loan from Danish stød.

parole.significato: stød
parole.testo: From Danish stød. Doublet of stöt.

parole.significato: pessimism
parole.testo: Compound of svart (“black”) + syn (“view”). Apparently a calque of Danish sortsyn, coined by Danish critic Georg Brandes in 1895. First attested in 1908.

parole.significato: only used in till syvende och sist
parole.testo: Borrowed from Danish syvende. Doublet of sjunde.

parole.significato: at the end of the day (when everything is taken into account)
parole.testo: Partial calque of Danish til syvende og sidst. Attested since 1915.

parole.significato: tomato
parole.testo: From Danish tomat, from Spanish tomate.

parole.significato: to do without, to dispense with
parole.testo: Borrowed from Danish undvære (equivalent to und- + vara), from Middle Low German untberen, entberen. Doublet of umbära. Compare German entbehren.

parole.significato: The letter Ö, as an (often jocular) replacement when referring to something considered (overly) Danish or Norwegian.
parole.testo: Unadapted borrowing from Danish ø and unadapted borrowing from Norwegian ø.
